X-rays were initially used to detect fractures, pneumonia, and other bone-related issues. However, their resolution was limited due to the limitations of early radiographic techniques.

In the 1970s, computed tomography (CT) emerged as a major advancement, providing cross-sectional images of the body. This technology significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and speed, particularly in emergency situations where quick diagnosis could save lives.

The 1980s witnessed the introduction of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which provided high-resolution images of soft tissues such as the brain, spinal cord, and muscles. This technology also allowed for detailed visualization of organs and structures within the body, enhancing the ability to diagnose neurological disorders, tumors, and vascular diseases.

In the 1990s, positron emission tomography (PET) came into play, enabling the visualization of metabolic processes within the body. PET scans could help identify areas of abnormal cell activity, aiding in the diagnosis and treatment planning of various cancers, neurological disorders, and heart diseases.

In recent years, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) has further transformed medical imaging. AI algorithms can analyze large datasets of medical images, identifying patterns and anomalies that might be missed by human eyes. This approach has the potential to significantly improve the efficacy of treatments while minimizing side effects.
